item.title: Sources & interpretations
item.description:
On this paper the interpretation question tests AO4 — how interpretations differ, why they differ, and which is more convincing. The key to why they differ is provenance: who wrote it, when, their background and purpose.

Below is the provenance of every interpretation AQA has set. Read it and ask: how might this author’s background, date and purpose explain the view they take?

2024

Interpretation A (Question 1)

Queen Elizabeth did not like Parliament. She only held one when she needed money. Her ideal Parliament gave her money and then went home. In short, the message was clear – shut up, pay up, pack up. But some MPs wanted to debate other things like marriage, the succession, religious reform, Mary, Queen of Scots, and foreign policy. Elizabeth's Parliaments were influenced, although never controlled, by members of her Privy Council, such as William Cecil. Parliamentary debate was not always kept on 'safe' issues but MPs strayed into areas defined as off-limits by Elizabeth.

Provenance: An interpretation of Queen Elizabeth and Parliament. Adapted from 'Elizabeth I – Profiles in Power' by Christopher Haigh, 1998.

item.title: Drake's Circumnavigation — Improved Navigation (2024)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far does a study of [historic site] support · AO1/AO2

The question

“Improved navigation was the main consequence of Drake’s voyage around the world, 1577–1580.” How far does a study of the Americas and Drake’s circumnavigation support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to the Americas and Drake’s circumnavigation and your contextual knowledge. [16 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I partially agree that improved navigation was a consequence of Drake’s circumnavigation, but a study of the voyage suggests that the acquisition of wealth, the challenge to Spanish power, and the boost to English national prestige and confidence were at least as important, and arguably more significant, consequences.

“Entertainment for all was the main consequence of the development of the Elizabethan theatre.” How far does a study of The Globe Theatre support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to The Globe Theatre and your contextual knowledge. [16 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I partially agree that ’entertainment for all’ was the main consequence of the Elizabethan theatre’s development, and a study of the Globe Theatre provides strong evidence for this. However, the Globe also demonstrates other important consequences: the creation of a new English literary tradition, the growth of commercial enterprise, and the sharpening of political and cultural tensions about the place of entertainment in Elizabethan society.

item.title: Kenilworth Castle — To Impress (2021)
item.description:
16-mark question · How far does a study of [historic site] support · AO1/AO2

The question

“The main reason for building a stately home in the Elizabethan period was to impress.” How far does a study of Kenilworth Castle support this statement? Explain your answer. You should refer to Kenilworth Castle and your contextual knowledge. [16 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

I strongly agree that Kenilworth Castle supports the view that the main reason for building and improving a stately home in the Elizabethan period was to impress, and in Kenilworth’s case specifically to impress the Queen. The evidence of Robert Dudley’s 19-day entertainment of Elizabeth in 1575 is the clearest possible illustration of a nobleman spending on an extraordinary scale to demonstrate his devotion, wealth, and importance to his monarch.

Model answer — Level 4

I partially agree that religion was a reason for helping the poor in Elizabethan England, and Lord Burghley’s almshouse provides some evidence for this view. However, a fuller study of the almshouse also reveals that personal legacy, family pride, and aristocratic fashion were equally important motivations, and that the government’s formal poor relief policies were driven more by fear of disorder than by religious charity.

item.title: Catholic Plots (2019)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about the Catholic plots against Queen Elizabeth I. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The Catholic plots against Elizabeth were important because they represented a genuine, sustained threat to her life and reign that forced a fundamental transformation in Elizabethan government. The key plots — the Ridolfi Plot (1571), the Throckmorton Plot (1583), and the Babington Plot (1586) — all shared the same basic structure: assassinate Elizabeth, replace her with the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots, and restore Catholicism to England with the backing of foreign Catholic powers. The Babington Plot came closest to success: Anthony Babington and his co-conspirators had obtained what they believed was Mary’s written approval for the plan. Francis Walsingham’s spy network intercepted the letters, and the exposure of this correspondence provided Elizabeth’s council with the evidence needed to execute Mary in February 1587. The plots mattered because they kept the threat of political assassination live for nearly two decades and forced Elizabeth to govern in a constant state of vigilance.

item.title: Catholic Plots Against Elizabeth (2021)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about Catholic plots against Queen Elizabeth I? Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretation A. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in identifying Mary Queen of Scots’ arrival as the starting point for the Catholic threat to Elizabeth. Foster argues that ‘Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England was a problem for Elizabeth’ and that ’the Northern Rebellion was an attempt to replace Elizabeth with Mary,’ which accurately reflects the political dynamic. Mary arrived in England in 1568 after fleeing Scotland, and her presence immediately created a danger: as a Catholic with a strong dynastic claim to the English throne (through Henry VIII’s sister Margaret), she became the natural figurehead for Catholic plots. The Northern Rebellion of 1569 was led by the Catholic earls of Northumberland and Westmorland and explicitly aimed to free Mary, marry her to the Duke of Norfolk, and put her on the throne. Although the rebellion failed — it was crushed without a major battle — it demonstrated that Mary’s mere presence in England was destabilising, a problem that was not resolved until her execution in 1587.

item.title: Catholic Plots Threatening Elizabeth (2024)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the ways in which Catholic plots threatened Queen Elizabeth. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Catholic plots threatened Queen Elizabeth by creating a sustained campaign of assassination attempts and conspiracies over nearly two decades, each of which drew in foreign powers and exploited the unresolved question of the succession. The Ridolfi Plot of 1571 was an early example: Roberto Ridolfi, an Italian banker, coordinated a plan involving the Duke of Norfolk (who would marry Mary Queen of Scots), the Duke of Alba’s Spanish army in the Netherlands, and a papal blessing to assassinate Elizabeth and place Mary on the throne. The plot was uncovered by Elizabeth’s spy network, and Norfolk was executed — but the episode demonstrated that the threat came from an international Catholic network willing to act against Protestant England. This led directly to Parliament passing the Recusancy Act of 1581, which increased fines for attending Catholic Mass and made harbouring Catholic priests an act of treason, showing how each plot forced the government into harder anti-Catholic positions.

item.title: Difficulties as Female Ruler (2021)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the difficulties which faced Queen Elizabeth as a female ruler. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Elizabeth faced profound difficulties as a female ruler because prevailing ideas in the sixteenth century held that women were intellectually, emotionally, and physically unsuited to govern. This view was most forcefully expressed by the Protestant reformer John Knox, whose pamphlet The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women (1558) argued that female rule was contrary to nature, divine law, and human law. Although Knox was targeting Mary Queen of Scots and the Catholic regents of Scotland, his arguments applied equally to Elizabeth. Within England, many councillors and subjects shared the assumption that a woman needed a husband to advise and guide her — which meant that the question of Elizabeth’s marriage was from the very beginning not just a personal matter but a constitutional pressure. Parliament repeatedly petitioned her to marry and settle the succession, and when she refused or delayed, some saw it as evidence of feminine indecision rather than deliberate policy.

item.title: Earl of Essex (2020)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Earl of Essex? Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretation A. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in portraying Essex as a man whose personal flaws fatally undermined his political position. Cavendish argues that Essex was ‘arrogant and reckless’ and ‘unwilling to be ruled by a woman,’ and this is well supported by the historical evidence. Essex repeatedly clashed with Elizabeth over authority and respect. Most dramatically, during a Privy Council meeting in 1598, he turned his back on the Queen — a profound act of disrespect — and she boxed his ears. Rather than apologising, Essex reached for his sword. This incident revealed a man whose pride could not accept subordination to a female monarch, regardless of the political cost. His behaviour showed the fundamental incompatibility between his own character and the essential requirement of Elizabethan court politics: total deference to the Queen.

item.title: Elizabeth and Parliament (2024)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about Queen Elizabeth and Parliament? Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretation A. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in arguing that Elizabeth called Parliament primarily for financial reasons and resented MPs debating matters she considered her prerogative. Haigh’s vivid summary — ‘shut up, pay up, pack up’ — captures an important truth about Elizabeth’s constitutional position. She summoned Parliament only 13 times over her 45-year reign, and in each case financial necessity played a major role: Parliament controlled the right to grant extraordinary taxation, which Elizabeth needed for war and defence. When MPs attempted to broaden debate into areas like the succession, marriage, or religious reform, Elizabeth was swift to close down discussion. In 1566, MPs petitioned Elizabeth to settle the succession and marry; she was furious and told them that her marriage was ’nothing meet for you to meddle with.’ In 1571, Peter Wentworth attempted to raise matters Elizabeth had forbidden discussion of and was sent to the Tower of London. These incidents confirm Haigh’s portrayal of a Queen determined to limit Parliament’s role.

item.title: Elizabethan Court (2019)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about the Elizabethan Court? Explain your answer using Interpretation A and your contextual knowledge. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in describing the Elizabethan Court as a centre of patronage and power because this accurately reflects how political life worked in Elizabethan England. Williams describes it as ‘a market place for patronage, combining formal ceremony with a scramble for status, influence and profit,’ and this captures the reality that access to Elizabeth and her court was the key to political survival. Patronage flowed from the monarch outwards — those who gained Elizabeth’s favour could receive lucrative government offices, monopolies, and titles. Robert Dudley, for example, was made Earl of Leicester through Elizabeth’s patronage and in turn extended patronage to his own clients, including writers and artists. Being excluded from court could be devastating: when the Earl of Essex stormed out of the Privy Council after a confrontation with Elizabeth in 1598, he effectively cut himself off from the patronage network that sustained him, which contributed directly to his disastrous rebellion in 1601.

item.title: Elizabethan Court (2022)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about Queen Elizabeth I’s court. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Queen Elizabeth I’s court was important because it was the centre of all political power in Elizabethan England. Unlike a modern government with fixed offices and departments, the Elizabethan court was not a place but a collection of people who surrounded the monarch wherever she went — from Whitehall and Hampton Court to the great country houses she visited on her summer progresses. Access to the Queen was everything: those who could speak to Elizabeth, catch her eye, or gain her trust could receive titles, offices, monopolies, and land. This system of patronage meant that every ambitious nobleman, lawyer, or soldier had to find a way into the court’s networks to advance themselves. The Privy Council — Elizabeth’s inner circle of advisers — met at court and managed the day-to-day business of government: foreign policy, taxation, defence, and religious affairs all passed through it. The court was therefore important not just as a social gathering but as the engine of Elizabethan government.

item.title: Elizabethan Golden Age (2021)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about Elizabethan England that made it a ‘Golden Age’. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The idea of a ‘Golden Age’ is important because it reflects the extraordinary cultural flourishing that took place in Elizabethan England, particularly in literature and drama. The period produced some of the greatest works in the English language: William Shakespeare wrote plays such as Hamlet, Romeo and Juliet, and A Midsummer Night’s Dream that explored universal human themes and are still performed worldwide today. Christopher Marlowe, Edmund Spenser, and Philip Sidney contributed poetry and plays of equal distinction. This cultural explosion was made possible by patronage — Elizabeth herself had an acting company (the Queen’s Men), while nobles like Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, sponsored writers and artists. The theatre industry grew rapidly: from the first purpose-built public theatre (simply called ‘The Theatre,’ built in 1576) to the Globe in 1599, theatrical entertainment became central to London life and attracted audiences of thousands daily. This cultural achievement was important because it established English as a literary language of European significance and created a legacy that has defined perceptions of the period ever since.

item.title: Elizabethan Theatre (2022)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about the theatre in Elizabethan England? Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretation A. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in describing the theatre as popular across social classes in Elizabethan England. The interpretation notes that ‘all sorts of people’ attended Elizabethan plays, and this is well supported by contextual knowledge. The design of theatres like the Globe (built 1599) deliberately catered for all social groups: groundlings — the poorest audience members — paid just one penny to stand in the yard directly in front of the stage, while wealthier patrons paid two or three pence for covered gallery seats with a clearer view. This mixed audience was unusual in Elizabethan society, where most social spaces strictly separated the classes. The sheer scale of theatre attendance — the Globe could hold up to 3,000 people — shows how central the theatre had become to London life by the end of Elizabeth’s reign, with theatres able to fill multiple times per week.

item.title: Elizabethan Theatre (2024)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about the theatre in Elizabethan England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The theatre was important in Elizabethan England because it was the most significant new cultural institution of the period, bringing together all social classes around a shared experience of entertainment and ideas. Before the Elizabethan theatre, dramatic performances had been religious mystery plays performed in town squares or short pieces performed at court for the nobility. The opening of the first purpose-built public theatre (‘The Theatre’) in 1576 in Shoreditch created something new: a permanent, commercial venue where anyone who could afford the entry price — as little as one penny for groundlings — could watch professional plays. By the 1590s, London had around a dozen theatres including the Rose, the Swan, and the Globe (built 1599), capable of drawing audiences of 2,000–3,000 people multiple times a week. The scale of this industry was extraordinary and made the theatre a central feature of Elizabethan urban life. The plays of Shakespeare, Marlowe, and Jonson engaged with politics, morality, love, and power in ways that made the theatre a forum for exploring the ideas of the age.

item.title: Elizabethan Voyages of Discovery (2023)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about the Elizabethan voyages of discovery. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The Elizabethan voyages of discovery were important because they transformed England’s economic position and established the foundations of a global trading empire. Francis Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe (1577–1580) was the most dramatic achievement of the period: sailing in the Golden Hind, Drake raided Spanish ports and treasure ships along the Pacific coast of South America, returning with plunder worth £160,000 — more than the Crown’s entire annual income at the time. Elizabeth’s share of the proceeds paid off the national debt. Drake was knighted on his return, and his voyage demonstrated that English ships and sailors could challenge Spain’s dominance of the world’s trade routes. The voyages also opened up commercial possibilities: the Muscovy Company (founded 1555), the Levant Company (1581), and the East India Company (1600) all grew from the expanding knowledge and confidence in English navigation that the voyages created.

item.title: Essex Rebellion (2023)
item.description:
8-mark question · Interpretations: how convincing · AO4a/AO4d

The question

How convincing is Interpretation A about Essex’s rebellion? Explain your answer based on your contextual knowledge and what it says in Interpretation A. [8 marks]

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing in arguing that the rivalry between Cecil and Essex, rather than Essex’s personal ambition alone, drove the rebellion. Haigh writes that ‘Elizabeth was unable to control the competition between Robert Cecil and the Earl of Essex’ and that ‘Elizabeth’s patronage increasingly favoured Cecil and his followers,’ and this is well supported by evidence. By the late 1590s, Robert Cecil had secured his dominance in government — he was effectively Elizabeth’s chief minister, managing affairs of state and controlling access to the Queen. Essex, despite his fame as a military hero and his genuine popularity with the London public, found himself increasingly frozen out. The revocation of his monopoly on the import of sweet wines in 1600 was devastating: Essex had used the income from this monopoly to sustain his large network of clients and supporters. Without patronage to distribute, his following would disintegrate. The rebellion in February 1601, when Essex led 300 men through the streets of London hoping to raise a popular uprising, was therefore driven by desperation rather than a carefully planned coup.

item.title: Lives of the Poor in Elizabethan England (2023)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the ways in which the lives of poor people changed in Elizabethan England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The lives of poor people in Elizabethan England changed as a result of worsening economic conditions during the period, which led in turn to new government policies that both restricted and attempted to help them. Economic change was not kind to the poor: inflation throughout the sixteenth century meant that prices rose faster than wages, reducing the purchasing power of ordinary labourers. The dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII had removed a significant source of charitable relief, since monasteries had traditionally fed and sheltered the poor. By the 1590s, a series of bad harvests between 1594 and 1598 caused genuine famine in parts of England. These changes led to a visible increase in the numbers of wandering vagrants — people who had lost their land through enclosures or their livelihoods through economic change, and who now moved around the country in search of work or food. The government’s initial response was harsh: the Vagabonds Act of 1572 ordered vagrants to be whipped and branded on first offence, reflecting the view that most vagabonds were idle by choice rather than necessity.

item.description:

Compare the levels below — same question, different grades. Notice what the higher-level answer does that the lower one doesn’t.

Model answer — Level 4

Interpretation A is convincing about the difficulties Elizabeth faced over marriage because it correctly identifies that the problem was political rather than personal. Williams argues that ‘it seems unlikely that she had a deep-seated personal dislike of marriage but choosing a husband was difficult,’ and this is supported by the evidence. Every serious suitor Elizabeth considered brought serious political dangers with him. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was politically toxic — he was widely suspected of arranging the death of his wife, Amy Robsart, in 1560, and marrying him would have made Elizabeth look complicit in a scandal. Foreign Catholic suitors like the Archduke Charles of Austria and the Duke of Anjou were unacceptable to Protestant councillors and Parliament, who feared the country would drift back towards Catholicism. Williams is right that the structural constraints made marriage nearly impossible to settle, whatever Elizabeth’s personal feelings.

item.title: Mary Queen of Scots Arrival (2018)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about the arrival of Mary, Queen of Scots in England in 1568. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The arrival of Mary Queen of Scots in England in 1568 was important because it immediately created a new and serious threat to Elizabeth’s security. Mary had been forced to abdicate the Scottish throne and flee to England after the murder of her husband Lord Darnley and her scandalous marriage to the suspected murderer, Bothwell, had turned Scottish nobles against her. Once in England, however, Mary became a dangerous rallying point for English Catholics, who regarded her as the legitimate heir to the English throne through her great-grandmother Margaret Tudor. Unlike Elizabeth, Mary was a devout Catholic, which made her the natural choice for those who wanted to restore Catholicism to England. Within months of her arrival, the Northern Rebellion of 1569 was launched by the Catholic earls of Northumberland and Westmorland with the explicit aim of freeing Mary, marrying her to the Duke of Norfolk, and placing her on the throne. The rebellion was crushed, but it demonstrated that Mary’s presence alone was destabilising English politics.

item.description:

Interpretation A is convincing in identifying worsening conditions in the later Elizabethan period as the driver of government action on poverty. Slack argues that ’there was price inflation, harvest failure and famine’ which led to ’large numbers of vagrants’ who ‘caused disorder,’ and this is well supported by contextual knowledge. The 1590s were a decade of genuine economic crisis: a series of harvest failures between 1594 and 1598 caused widespread famine in parts of England, and the long wars against Spain placed an enormous financial burden on the population through taxation. Inflation, driven partly by the influx of New World silver, had eroded the purchasing power of ordinary wages throughout the century. The result was a visible increase in the numbers of wandering poor, which alarmed property owners and local authorities. Slack is right that fear of disorder — rather than simple charity — was a major motivation for the government’s response.

item.title: Poverty Relief and Poor Laws (2019)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how poverty was dealt with during the reign of Queen Elizabeth I. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Poverty was dealt with during Elizabeth’s reign through a gradual shift from local, charitable solutions to a nationally legislated system of poor relief. In the early part of the reign, relief for the poor depended largely on church collections, private charity, and the efforts of individual towns and parishes. Some towns, notably Norwich, developed sophisticated local schemes in the 1570s that distinguished between different types of poor people: those who genuinely could not work (the ‘impotent poor’ — the elderly, sick, and very young) were given relief, while the able-bodied unemployed were set to work, and ‘vagabonds’ who refused to work were punished. The Norwich scheme was significant because it showed that organised, systematic poor relief could work and provided a model for later national legislation.

item.title: Puritanism (2020)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about Puritanism in Elizabethan England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

Puritanism was important in Elizabethan England because it represented the most significant internal challenge to Elizabeth’s Religious Settlement and revealed the limits of her ability to control the Church of England. The Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 had deliberately tried to create a broad Protestant Church that could accommodate a range of views, but Puritans — who wanted a more thoroughly Protestant, Calvinist church purged of all Catholic practices — found it unsatisfactory. Puritans objected to the continued use of vestments (clerical robes they associated with Catholicism), to the hierarchical structure of bishops, and to the use of the traditional liturgy. The Vestments Controversy of the 1560s saw clergy refusing to wear the required dress, forcing Archbishop Parker to issue the Advertisements of 1566 ordering conformity. More radically, the ‘Prophesyings’ of the 1570s — unauthorised meetings where ministers gathered to discuss scripture — alarmed Elizabeth so much that she ordered Archbishop Grindal to suppress them; when he refused, she suspended him for seven years. Puritanism was important because it forced Elizabeth to define and defend the limits of the Settlement repeatedly throughout her reign.

item.title: Spanish Armada (2025)
item.description:
8-mark question · Explain what was important about · AO1/AO2

The question

Explain what was important about the Spanish Armada. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The Spanish Armada was important in the immediate term because its defeat removed the most serious military threat Elizabeth had faced and secured England’s survival as a Protestant nation. Philip II of Spain had assembled a fleet of 130 ships carrying around 17,000 soldiers with the aim of transporting the Duke of Parma’s army across the English Channel to invade England, overthrow Elizabeth, and restore Catholicism. The English fleet under Lord Howard of Effingham and Drake used faster, more manoeuvrable ships and the tactic of fireships to scatter the Armada at Gravelines in August 1588. Bad weather off the Scottish and Irish coasts destroyed around half the Spanish fleet on the return journey. The victory ended the immediate invasion threat and demonstrated that England could defend itself against the greatest military power in Europe. Elizabeth’s famous speech at Tilbury — ‘I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman, but I have the heart and stomach of a king’ — became one of the defining statements of her reign and reinforced her image as a monarch capable of defending her people.

item.title: Spanish Armada Defeat (2022)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of how the Spanish Armada was defeated. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The Spanish Armada was defeated through a combination of English tactical skill and Spanish command failures that came together decisively at the Battle of Gravelines in August 1588. The Armada’s plan required the fleet to sail up the English Channel, rendezvous with the Duke of Parma’s army in the Spanish Netherlands, and transport approximately 27,000 troops across the Channel to invade England. The plan depended on everything going according to Philip II’s instructions, but communication failures between Medina Sidonia (the Armada’s inexperienced commander) and Parma meant that when the Armada arrived off Calais, Parma’s army was not ready. This delay allowed the English to use fireships — unmanned burning vessels sent into the anchored Spanish fleet — at Gravelines on the night of 7–8 August. The Spanish ships cut their anchor cables in panic and scattered, breaking the tight defensive formation that had made the Armada difficult to attack in the Channel. English warships then attacked the disorganised fleet, inflicting significant damage and casualties.

item.title: Theatre Development (2020)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the ways in which the theatre developed in Elizabethan England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The theatre developed in Elizabethan England from informal performances in inn courtyards and guild halls into a major commercial industry based around purpose-built public theatres. The critical breakthrough came in 1576 when James Burbage built ‘The Theatre’ in Shoreditch, just outside the City of London’s jurisdiction — the first permanent public theatre in England. This development transformed the economics of drama: instead of relying on the goodwill of innkeepers or the patronage of a single noble, acting companies could now earn regular income from paying audiences. The success of The Theatre inspired rivals, and within years the Curtain theatre and then the Rose (1587) and the Swan had been built, creating a competitive theatrical market in London. The construction of the Globe in 1599, built by Shakespeare’s company the Chamberlain’s Men using the timber from the demolished Theatre, represented the culmination of this physical development — a large, well-equipped venue capable of staging the elaborate productions Shakespeare’s plays required.

item.title: Threats to the Religious Settlement (2025)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the threats to the Elizabethan religious settlement in England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 — which established a Protestant Church of England with Elizabeth as Supreme Governor — faced threats from both Catholics who wanted to restore the old faith and Puritans who thought the Settlement had not gone far enough in reforming the Church. The Catholic threat was the most immediately dangerous. Pope Pius V’s issue of the Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis in 1570 excommunicated Elizabeth and formally released her Catholic subjects from their loyalty to her, transforming Catholic religious practice from mere dissent into potential treason. This was reinforced by the arrival of Jesuit and seminary priests — trained at colleges in Douai and Rome — who entered England secretly to minister to Catholics and keep the old faith alive. The government responded by making it a treasonable offence to harbour priests, and many, including Edmund Campion, were executed. The Northern Rebellion of 1569 and the subsequent Catholic plots showed that these threats had real political dimensions: they aimed not just to preserve Catholic worship but to overthrow the Settlement entirely by replacing Elizabeth with the Catholic Mary Queen of Scots.

item.title: Voyages of Discovery Impact (2018)
item.description:
8-mark question · Write an account of · AO1/AO2

The question

Write an account of the ways in which the voyages of discovery affected Elizabethan England. [8 marks]

Model answer — Level 4

The voyages of discovery affected Elizabethan England most dramatically by bringing enormous wealth into the country and transforming the financial power of the Crown. Francis Drake’s circumnavigation of the globe between 1577 and 1580 involved raiding Spanish ports and treasure ships along the Pacific coast of South America. When he returned on the Golden Hind, the plunder he carried was worth approximately £160,000 — more than the Crown’s annual income at the time. Elizabeth took a substantial share, which allowed her to pay off significant national debt. This sudden influx of wealth enabled the government to fund further ventures and strengthened England’s financial position relative to its rivals. Drake’s success also led directly to further profitable privateering voyages, and Elizabeth’s decision to knight Drake on his return ship confirmed the voyages’ importance as a source of both wealth and national prestige, sending a clear message to Spain that England would challenge its monopoly on Atlantic trade.

item.title: Why Were the Spanish Defeated
item.description:
What happened & why it matters

  • Fireship attack (7 Aug 1588)
    • At the time — broke the Spanish formation
    • Long term — exposed Spanish ships to English gunnery
  • Battle of Gravelines (8 Aug 1588)
    • At the time — English long-range gunnery damaged many Spanish ships
    • Long term — Armada had to retreat; storms finished the job
  • Elizabeth at Tilbury (8 Aug 1588)
    • At the time — famous speech boosted morale
    • Long term — became defining image of Elizabethan strength
